extract:
Pete Townshend was born on 19 May 1945 in Chiswick, west London, to a musical family. His father Cliff played saxophone with the RAF dance band the Squadronaires and his mother Betty was a singer. Raised in Acton, he attended Acton County Grammar School alongside John Entwistle and later studied at Ealing Art College. That art-school environment exposed him to auto-destructive art theory, which fed directly into his guitar-smashing stage act. Although he is best known as the principal songwriter and guitarist of the Who, whom he has led since the mid-1960s, he has maintained a parallel solo career stretching from the early 1970s to the present.

The Who grew out of the Detours, a band fronted by Roger Daltrey. With Keith Moon on drums, they briefly became the High Numbers before settling on their permanent name under managers Kit Lambert and Chris Stamp. They became the house band of the London mod scene. Townshend's formative influences ranged from American R&B and Link Wray to jazz. From 1967 onward he was also shaped by the teachings of the Indian spiritual master Meher Baba, whose influence runs through Tommy, Lifehouse, and much of his solo work.

His first widely released solo album, Who Came First (1972), grew out of devotional records he had made for Baba followers. It mixed home demos such as "Pure and Easy" and "Let's See Action" with Ronnie Lane's "Evolution" and a cover of Jim Reeves' "There's a Heartache Following Me." Rough Mix (1977), a duet album with Lane produced by Glyn Johns, featured Eric Clapton, Charlie Watts and John Entwistle. Its looser, rootsier sound shows on tracks like "Street in the City" and "My Baby Gives It Away." Empty Glass (1980), produced by Chris Thomas and released in the US on Atco, was his commercial peak. It included "Let My Love Open the Door," a US top ten hit, along with "Rough Boys" and "A Little Is Enough." Thomas also produced the denser All The Best Cowboys Have Chinese Eyes (1982), which included "Slit Skirts." The Scoop series (1983, 1987, 1994) gathered demos that revealed how fully he sketched Who songs at home.

The mid-1980s brought more conceptual projects. White City: A Novel (1985) arrived with an accompanying film and the single "Face the Face." Deep End Live! (1986) documented a big-band touring ensemble that included David Gilmour. The Iron Man (1989), adapted from Ted Hughes' children's story, featured John Lee Hooker and Nina Simone. Psychoderelict (1993) was a radio-play-style concept album about an aging rock star. That same year, the Broadway production of The Who's Tommy won Tony Awards, including one for Townshend's score. The stage work later spawned international productions such as the German-language recording released in 2015. Also in 2015, Classic Quadrophenia recast his 1973 rock opera orchestrally, with Alfie Boe singing the lead.

Critics have long regarded Townshend as one of rock's most ambitious songwriters. He is credited with popularizing the rock opera and pioneering feedback, power chords and the windmill guitar style. Players from Paul Weller to the punk generation have cited him as an influence. He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame with the Who in 1990 and received Kennedy Center Honors in 2008.

Townshend published his memoir, Who I Am, in 2012 and his first novel, The Age of Anxiety, in 2019. That same year he and Daltrey released the Who album WHO, and he has continued to tour with the band. His legacy rests both on the Who's canon and on a solo body of work that exposes the more intimate, searching side of his writing.
title: Pete Townshend
